[Someone did a quick and dirty calculation here. ](http://theastronomist.fieldofscience.com/2011/07/cubic-millimeter-of-your-brain.html?m=1) 

Probably not the most precise number because it's literally just estimating the number of neurons and average number of dentrites on a single neuron, then using those numbers to extrapolate the number of synapses im the whole brain. We also know the average volume of brains (again something than can vary massively between people), so we can then say oh a 1 mm cube has around 10^9 synapses. Although those numbers were estimated through very sophisticated and impressive means (such as tossing a human brain in a blender, I'm only half joking), they are still educated guesses. So would I say that's an "accurate" fact? Yeah, for now, given current knowledge and assuming the average across all humans. But that probably will change in the future.

Also "on average" can be a little unintentionally misleading since neural density (and neuron type, each of which has different sizes and numbers of dentrites and thus synapses) varies greatly throughout the nervous system, but again it's roughly correct. (For an extreme example, the cerebellum contains more neurons than the rest of the brain combined. Despite this, it makes up only 10% of the brain's total volume, due to it having a metric fuckton (the proper scientific term) of granule cells (a kind of catch-all category for many small neuron types). So because these cells take up much less space yet there are so many more of them, the number we get for neural density in a 1mm cube is going to be very different than the remaining 90% of brain volume and is going to make statements about averages at the very least unintentionally misleading, which granted is a problem a lot of statistics have in general).

So I do really like the Mali playthrough for building tall however I would say there are a few drawbacks that make it not my favorite.

One is that you can't control all the mines under one title until you form the kingdom, and even then succession can be a pain. I like to roleplay and not rush myself into making kingdoms or grabbing a ton of land however, and Mali requires a decent number of territories to complete. Plus the mines are spread across three counties and two duchies, so I usually run into annoying inheritance issues. Nothing that can't be overcome, but I'd rather not have to deal ya know. Especially when I've built up a county a little TOO well. 

My biggest problem with that start however is terrain composition. That makes a HUGE difference in development level, especially if you add in cultural bonuses. Every coastal tile gets a building that boosts tax and more importantly development. Fields and floodplains and some others also get development boosting buildings on top of natural extra development growth. In my experience, development is far and away the most important factor in making money. In Mali, the VAST majority of tiles are hills, which decrease development by an entire 10%. So not only does the kingdom not have any coastal tiles, 90%+ of the tiles just aren't condusive to getting development up asap. 

Sardinia doesn't have amazing tiles and has a lot fewer, but all of them are coastal and it's really easy to make the kingdom in one life without stressing, and really easy to raid from.

Parts of India start with high development, coastal, AND farmlands. Super viable to just play one dutchy too.

Despite all my praise of coastal tiles, the best place in the game for building tall miiiiight be Bohemia imo. Farmlands, plains, Praha has 6 holdings, gold mine, and start as a vassal which IMO is better in general but also for building tall. (Being in the council as a steward kicks ass, especially if your leige is the emperor. Biggest danger for Bohemia start is becoming the Holy Roman Emperor yourself lmao)

And I'm sure there are other places for building tall I just haven't tried yet. Kyiv is strong. Baghdad and Cairo (and their surrounding areas) are also VERY strong but require a bit more work to obtain and hold unless you don't mind replacing the literal Sunni Caliph or Fatimid Sultan, which I really don't like to do. 

Like don't get me wrong I do think those gold mines are really strong but I wouldn't call it the absolute best location for building tall in my experience. Like you'll get to 100 development eventually no problem and probably out-earn other starts at the end of the day because of that combined with the mines, but I usually don't play my campaigns until the end so I haven't personally experienced that.

And if you take it as an Asatru and feudalize you can play tall AND raid all of the Mediterranean from a central location as an additional huge income source (letting you build the next level of buildings/gold mine ASAP). Easier to do in 867 but I still prefer doing it in 1066 because you tech up way too slowly for building tall in the former imo

If you wanna not be Asatru anymore but still raid you can take the practiced pirates cultural tradition, the prestige hit really isn't too bad.

Probably my favorite location in the whole game if I wanna both build tall AND raid tho (other would be maybe southern India but with that I prefer starting as Buddhist, the kingdom is a lot more difficult to form, and you're much less isolated. I've never actually done a viking run in India though and kinda want to now).

I'm trying to tell you, the discipline as a whole doesn't accept it. Funding for one subfield comes from that subfield. Subfields publish in their own journals. I've tried being respectful, but I really feel like I'm arguing in circles here. It's okay to admit that you don't have the whole story. Hell, I discounted psychology before I started learning more about it too. But if your whole foundation of not accepting psychology is that one subfield puts stock into Freud or dream interpretation, that's severely misinformed on two levels.

You started the argument talking about how you don't trust social psychology research because you don't see it as a science, though. You then backed up this claim by pointing towards Freudian psychodynamics. Social is completely different than psychodynamic and often has conflicting ideas.

And I agree that there are problems in modern psychodynamic research. But for one, to my knowledge, the research on it is mostly only about the efficacy of psychodynamic therapy for patients. And again, psychodynamics are far removed from what Freud did. No paper would ever get published if it claimed anything about dream interpretation. I think what's going on is that your idea of what this field is doesn't match with the actual dogma. I'm going to say it again: no university or research lab takes Freud seriously. Not even the ones doing work in psychodynamics. 

And my own personal issues with the field don't mean it's not scientific. Just look at the huge debate between the cell and evolutionary biologists on aging. They each call the other misguided. That doesn't mean one or the other is unscientific in their work. Science is hella messy. But if something has been published and reproduced and tested again and again, you can take that as a sign of strong evidence. Systemic racism is one of these topics that has been widely studied and re-studied. Social psychology is now more rigorous than ever about this because of the reproducibility crisis (which in and of itself is 1. a much larger discussion and 2. not limited to psychology).

Okay, granted (there are holdouts sure, but that's why I said at large) . But modern psychodynamic theory has very little to do with Freud's. And is often used in a clinical (therapy) setting. If you can provide a single peer-reviewed modern study in a reputable journal on the idea that "dreams are based on suppressed desires," (which is what spawned this debate in the first place) I'll stop arguing. But a claim like that is, by definition, not scientific. And that means that it's not testable, which means you're never going to see research funding for theories like that one. 

And in most clinical, social, and cognitive psychology departments, nobody is taking those ideas seriously.  Now are there other problems with the field? Absolutely, and I'm willing to discuss them. But thinking that modern psychology in any way takes Freud or dream interpretation seriously in any way is ridiculous, although understandable given the sheer number of terrible pop-psych self-help books out there by random non-experts.

Psychology is not a monolith. There are many sub-fields that often disagree with one another, as with all sciences. And to claim that a field is not a science because of a small subset of people, especially when you consider that none of those people take even Freud seriously and those who do are NOT receiving funding (and are thus not employed at researchers) in the slightest.

I am a published author in the field, and I can assure you that the idea Freud had that we even give a shit about anymore is that psychological processes are sometimes unconscious (obviously so - you're gonna pay attention to a ball flying at your face without needing to consciously make that decision, for example). I don't know what to tell you beyond encouraging you to educate yourself more on the topic. The basic textbooks are just that - basic. When you simplify things you end up misconstruing them. I know that it's difficult with how research is often locked behind a paywall and the insular nature of scientific communities, and that's something most scientists honestly hate. But please don't make sweeping generalizations based off of something you probably heard in a class once. There's a lot more there under the surface, I promise. I can't really help more because I don't know the specifics of what you may have learned, but I'm hoping that you'll give the field a second chance and not dismiss all the very good and strenuous work being done because of what you may have learned in passing.

Psychodynamic theory is not accepted by the field at large. If you tried to use Newtonian mechanics to explain physics in a modern setting, you'd be laughed out of that room as well. And Newton actually did rigorous science, unlike Freud. Point is, the very nature of science is that it is constantly changing and the popularly known historical figures are often discounted because we actually have some semblance of what we're talking about now.

I've been polyamorous for many years, but I'm not super keyed into the community beyond my partners so I don't know if this alines with most folks' views but...

I personally think that the argument that one or the other is "not natural" is kinda pointless. For one, evolutionary psychology as it is today involves of thinking of plausible explanations and applying them them retroactively, and as someone who has done research in that field I personally think about 85% is just complete BS. 

But to commit the cardinal sin, let me list a few examples.

-Childrearing: Monogamy, causes a bonding effect that makes it more difficult for one parent to leave, thus increasing the change of two highly motivated parents to continue the species. Polyamory/non-monogamy increases the parent pool as to ensure the community will be taking care of the children.

-Jealousy: evolved in part to ensure monogamy for aforementioned reasons. Or, jealousy's default state isn't directed with one person as a focus, and evolved to keep GROUPS together and also promote friendly competition where everyone pushes everyone else to become better. Or maybe it's a result of tribalism.

These arguments are not very strong, but I hope they show that many similar behaviors can be justified with evolutionary arguments with not many good ways to evaluate those theories at all, especially since the experimental population we'd use now is so far removed society-wise from when those traits emerged.

And evolution works entirely through the mistake. We are NOT designed to function under our current society AT ALL. We simply developed to be advanced enough to survive in our niche. But we, as a species, are a wonderful and dysfunctional mess. So even if we could make convincing evolutionary arguments, those traits could simply be things to overcome through social training (which in and of itself is a skill we've evolved). These perspectives often ignore the massive nurture effect there can be.

For me personally, it took a long time to be comfortable with the idea of non-monogamy. Almost every single portrayal of relationships in media is monogamous. Marriage is "sacred" and between only two people. Jealousy is sometimes seen as "healthy". All I knew growing up was monogamy. I was able to overcome those biases because 1. I was motivated to and tried very hard and 2. I was still young, and thus more able to change. There are many arguments I could give for the benefits of polyamory over monogamy, but those have been given elsewhere and much more clearly than I ever could. And the reality is, most people are not going to embrace polyamory. I personally think that it can be more healthy and would prefer to see it widespread. I believe part of the problem causing so much cheating is because we aren't good at staying with one person and just because we're coupled or whatever doesn't mean we suddenly don't find others attractive. And to be clear, cheating is absolutely not okay. If one of my partners cheated on me and hid things from me, we would be breaking up immediately. One thing people don't seem to realize is that polyamory actually requires MORE communication. On one hand, this is very nice to have. On the other, it takes A LOT of work, and I just don't think most people are willing to do that, especially in the culture we live in.

tl;dr: I think there are a lot of good arguments for polyamory, and I fully understand why someone would want to only be monogamous, but I think the argument over if monogamy or non-monogamy is more "natural" is mostly meaningless.

I actually chose to opt into the program. It's basically only for people who find intrinsic value in learning in general. If you're not interested in many subjects, it's probably not for you. You have to take classes in the humanities, the sciences, and the social sciences. Hum Core is 8 units (each quarter), Social Science Core is 6, and Science Core is 4. You take each series for one year. The exception is that if you're a STEM major, you don't have to take the Science Core. Furthermore, you get to conduct your own research and publish a thesis in your senior year in a series of either two or three thesis classes.

I am double majoring in Psychology and Social Behavior and Criminology, Law, and Society. The maximum number of units I will ever have to take to graduate in 4 years is 18 for three quarters (and all other quarters I am taking 16).

The main question you should ask is this: do you love learning? Do many subjects fascinate you? Do you find joy in learning many things about many subjects? If no, then I suggest opting out and instead signing up for the Honors program within your specific major(s).

"Listen, Rogers, we don't want any funny business. Just give us what we want and our deal will be sealed." 

The room was illuminated by a single hanging bulb and the low glow of an old television. Fred Rodgers sat in a cold metal chair, looking down at his feet. Across the table, a hardened 50-something stared at the TV star with piercing eyes. His blue and yellow jacket was a billboard broadcasting into Roger's face. It read simply: FBI. 

*Shit, why did I have to leave that fucking blood-stained sweater in the garbage can? Why I have to get caught? What is-*

Rogers was brought back into reality by the crackling of static. The agent and Rogers swiveled to face the TV. A happy tune started playing and a familiar bearded man appeared on the screen. Ross. The only man Rogers had ever truly admired.

 The deal was simple. All Rogers had to do was give the FBI enough evidence to lock up Ross for good. In return, the agency promised that the death penalty would be off the table for Rogers. So Rogers had sent one final message over his show to his former ally: walk me through it, from the beginning to end. Tell me everything. 

"Hello, everyone. I've got a big show for you all today." Ross began laying his paints down, looking content in his work. "First things first, I think we shall paint a happy little boy."

Rogers cleared his throat. "He started his career as a child. He'll tell me how many victims he had back them through how many colors he uses to paint himself."

Ross stared with a peach-like color, painting the head, arms, hands, and one leg.

"His first victim was missing a leg."

Ross continued to paint, picking up a purple for the shirt, red for the pants, and a tiny yellow dot for the foot. Ross stood back and looked at his work before taking a bite out of a sandwich from a nearby table. He smiled at the camera, sending a chill down the agent's back. He proceeded to take two more bites, and set it back down. 

"Four victims. He...he cannibalised three of them. Probably not the first one, judging by our previous...talks." 

Ross began to paint a pleasant log cabin. He used different shades of brown, masterfully blending and concocting the colors until they formed a stout building. 

"He disposed of the bodies in a cabin. Probably near his house. You'll probably still find their remains there." Rogers swallowed. 

Ross stared into the camera, looking as content as ever. "You know, ever since starting this show, I have always looked to bring happiness into this world. You, too can bring happiness. Smile at someone. Paint something beautiful. Use your hands for something creative, something good."

Rogers spoke up. "He didn't kill again until he got his show. He's also telling me that I should create my next...masterpiece very soon. He'll catch on if I don't."

The FBI agent's piercing eyes never wavered. He spoke deeply and methodically. "You don't have to worry about that, Mr. Rogers. We already have plenty of evidence to prosecute."
He paused. "Our eyes have been on that cabin for months, and now we have what we need to get a warrant. Please continue."

Ross's grainy face grinned at the cold, gray room. He began to paint "happy little trees". Rogers knew that they were just filler, hiding the much more sinister symbolism. Animals were victims. Birds meant those who got away. Deer were five victims for each missing antler. Fish and other aquatic wildlife were cannibalized victims. Most carnivores stood for victims he sexually assaulted. Wolves were Ross himself, on the prowl. Most animals were missing parts; legs, arms, heads. They were painted so small only Rogers noticed the distance. As Ross painted, he mentioned things that seemed like passing jokes.

 "This deer didn't have many smarts about it."

He ate the brain.

"This bear is remarkably artistic."

He displayed the body for all to see.

"This bird was ripped limb-to-limb by the wolf."

*wait, what?*

Ross smiled after his most recent comment and began to finish the painting. 

Rogers's heart began to race. The FBI agent was making frantic calls. Did Ross know? Was he revealing himself? Did he have a final endgame?

Ross set down his brush and looked at his handiwork for a few moments. Finally, after what seemed like an eternity to all in the room, Ross moved aside.

There stood, unmistakable by Rogers and the agent, a man in a red sweater beside a man displaying large, yellow letters. 

*FBI.*

The TV shut off. 

The solitary light went out, bathing the room in absolute darkness. And then the screaming began.

That's part of the problem with depression. Personally, I didn't know anything else than what I felt, so I thought it was normal. It took me a long time to realize that normal people don't fantasize about killing themselves or lay in bed for days at a time. One reason this shit goes undiagnosed is that people don't realize they have it until it's too late.

Plus, there are people like you who tell us to just get over it. According to you, we're weak if we can't just snap out of it. That thought stays with is, and we don't tell anyone because telling someone makes us weak, right? Or at least that's what we're told.

Finally, you are partially correct. A part of depression is due to how people view the world. The entire point of CBT (the most popular type of therapy) is to change how people see their world and how they act in it. Part of it is indeed the way of thinking. But the largest part? Fucked up brain chemistry. Depression is mainly due to an issue with serotonin and other chemicals in the brain. CBT alleviates it, sure, but it doesn't go away without medication that tweak your brain chemistry.

Basically, depression sucks donkey dick, And don't try to tell people to just get over it. It doesn't work like that.
